extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in political economy, economic history, and colonial trade policy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for evaluating colonial governance and commercial regulation (late 18th-century perspective), including trade monopolies, market access for colonial produce, fiscal burdens, administrative structure, and treatment of slaves. Useful for assessing how mother-country policies affect colonial improvement and welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frugality of civil establishments
rubrics_metrics.description: The civil establishments in the English colonies cost relatively little (example totals cited), demonstrating 'at how small an expense three millions of people may not only be governed but well governed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether colonial civil government is conducted with modest expense (limited ceremonial and parade) and whether defence/protection burdens fall upon the mother country; examples contrast English frugality with more expensive ceremonials elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frugality of ecclesiastical government
rubrics_metrics.description: English colonial ecclesiastical government is frugal: 'Tithes are unknown among them; and their clergy... are maintained either by moderate stipends, or by the voluntary contributions of the people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the church imposes compulsory burdens (tithes, large stipends) or is supported modestly/voluntarily; impacts on public expense and social burden should be noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of expensive ceremonial and pomp
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonial upon the reception of a new governor or opening an assembly is 'sufficiently decent' but 'not accompanied with any expensive pomp or parade.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure whether official ceremonials create significant one-off or recurring costs and whether they encourage luxury and private extravagance among colonists (seen as a tax on the rich that spreads costly habits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecclesiastical oppression (tithes and mendicant orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Spanish and Portuguese colonies the ecclesiastical government is extremely oppressive: 'Tithes take place in all of them... oppressed with a numerous race of mendicant friars' whose beggary is 'a most grievous tax upon the poor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the degree to which religious institutions extract compulsory payments, monopolize land, or impose charitable duties that act as regressive taxes on the poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade monopoly by exclusive companies
rubrics_metrics.description: Some nations 'have given up the whole commerce of their colonies to an exclusive company' which forces colonists to buy/sell only through the company, degrading the value of colonial produce and stunting growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify existence and effects of company monopolies: inflated prices for imports, depressed prices for colonial exports, discouraged increases in production, and overall inhibition of colony development (examples: Holland historically, Portugal recently).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction of colonial trade to particular home ports (licensed fleets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other nations confined trade 'to a particular port of the mother country' with licensed fleets or special seasons, producing de facto cartel behavior among merchants and 'exorbitant and oppressive' profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess licensing/port restrictions that enable merchant collusion, raise prices, limit supply to colonies, and effectively operate like an exclusive company even without formal monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open intra-mother-country competition in colonial trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Where trade is free to all native merchants from different ports, the 'number and dispersed situation' of traders prevents combination and excessive profits, enabling colonies to buy cheaper and sell better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value competition among mother-country merchants as a criterion for reasonable colonial prices and better supply; examples: English policy (post-Plymouth) and France after dissolution of Mississippi company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market access for surplus produce (enumerated vs non-enumerated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Colonies allowed an extensive market for surplus produce fare better; enumerated commodities are confined to the home market, non-enumerated may be exported more widely (with ship restrictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine which colonial commodities are enumerated (forced into mother-country market) versus non-enumerated (freeer export) and how that affects prices received by colonists and incentives for cultivation or improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing export markets for staples (grain, lumber, cattle, fish) to promote improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting wide markets for grain, lumber, cattle, and fish raises their prices in colonies, facilitating land clearing, improvement, and provision for growing population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether policies grant broad markets to primary staples; assess effects on land clearing, settlement, and alignment of cattle/corn price ratios necessary for land improvement. Note negative effects when items are enumerated (e.g., hides added to enumeration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement of fisheries for naval and shipping power
rubrics_metrics.description: Encouraging colonial fisheries (e.g., New England) increases shipping and naval power; colonies often flourished without bounties that the mother country paid domestically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure statutory encouragements (or lack thereof) for fisheries and their contributions to maritime capacity and colonial export diversification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on colonial manufacture of refined goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Mother-country policies often reserve 'more advanced or more refined manufactures' (e.g., sugar refining, steel furnaces, slit-mills) to themselves by high duties or absolute prohibitions, preventing colonial manufacture even for local consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess prohibitions/duties that prevent establishment of refining or advanced manufactures in colonies, their impact on local industry, and whether they are justified by current colony economics or simply serve metropolitan manufacturers' jealousy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on interprovincial/internal colonial trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Britain prohibited exportation from one province to another by water and even carriage by land of certain goods (hats, wools, woollen goods), preventing the establishment of manufactures for distant sale within the colonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for internal trade prohibitions that fragment markets and impede the scaling of colonial manufactures beyond household or local levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawbacks on duties for re-exported foreign goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Great Britain allowed drawbacks (often half or more of duty) on foreign goods re-exported to colonies so they would not be prohibitively expensive; reductions in these drawbacks (e.g., 1763 statute) made colonies pay more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate extent of duty-drawback regimes for goods destined to colonies and whether diminished drawbacks increase colonial costs and reduce carrying trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of metropolitan merchants on colonial regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many regulations were devised with 'the merchants who carry it on' as principal advisers; their interest often prevailed over that of the colonies or mother country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whose interests shaped trade regulations—merchant lobbies vs broader public interest—and whether rules reflect narrow profit incentives (e.g., exclusive supply privileges, drawbacks to benefit merchants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of colonial political self-government
rubrics_metrics.description: English colonists enjoy near-complete liberty to manage their own affairs (assemblies with right to impose taxes, assemblies overseeing executive including appointment of some officers and sometimes governors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutional features: representative assemblies, taxation authority, appointment powers, oversight of revenue officers, and how these constrain the executive and protect colonists' rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political equality and absence of hereditary nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: Colonies generally lack hereditary nobility; social respect for old families exists but without privileges. Some councils are chosen rather than appointed, leading to greater equality and 'more republican' manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure presence/absence of hereditary privileges, appointment vs election of councils, and overall social equality as factors in colonial governance quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the metropolitan government (absolute vs free) and its colonial effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute governments (Spain, Portugal, France) exercise discretionary power in colonies leading to greater tyranny in remote provinces; free governments (England) afford greater security to distant inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the metropolitan constitutional character and how its mechanisms of oversight (or lack thereof) affect the safety, justice, and administrative violence in colonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal protection and management of slaves
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'good management' of slaves and legal protections (even weak) increase slaves' usefulness and fidelity; arbitrarily governed colonies may offer better judicial protection to slaves than fully free polities where masters are politically influential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess laws and magistrates' willingness to protect slaves against extreme abuse, and whether such protections improve the condition, intelligence, and productivity of enslaved laborers (comparison: French vs English planters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of capital for colonial improvement (local accumulation vs metropolitan remittances)
rubrics_metrics.description: The stock that has improved French sugar colonies was 'raised almost entirely from the gradual improvement and cultivation of those colonies.' English sugar colonies have received a great part of their stock sent out from England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether colonial investment comes from internal accumulation (suggesting sustainable local development) or primarily from metropolitan capital flows (which may affect long-term economic independence and patterns of development).
